19826-the-white-christmas-and-other-merr:
The White Christmas gathers merry Christmas plays for amateur performance. Its notes point performers to Denison's Songs Worth While for music. Most carol tunes are familiar to everyone, the editor says. Unfamiliar hymn music can be found in that collection. The volume itself is handsomely printed on non-glossy paper. It measures seven by ten and a quarter inches, bound in stout paper.

Schools, churches, and families staged Christmas plays every December. Publishers like Denison built catalogs for those stages. A white Christmas on stage needs songs everyone can sing. These plays mix sentiment, snow, and goodwill in short acts. The practical notes show the trade behind the tinsel. It is a handbook for homemade holiday theater.
19834-ethel-morton-s-holidays:
Mabell S. C. Smith wrote the Ethel Morton books for girls. Ethel Morton's Holidays, dated 1915, finds the Morton circle at leisure. Helen and Ethel Brown have gone to the West Woods. A wild grapevine there still holds yellow leaves bright enough for decorating. Tomorrow evening's plans send the girls hunting color. Roger accounts for his sisters with a brother's economy.

The Ethel books follow two cousins both named Ethel. Holidays mean clubs, crafts, parties, and small schemes. Smith fills them with doings girls could copy at home. Decorating with grape leaves is typical of the series. Its world is safe, busy, and friendly. Such series trained steady girl readers by the shelf.
19855-louis-school-days-a-story-for-boys:
E. J. May wrote Louis' School Days as a story for boys with a Christian aim. Its ideal schoolboy has affections restored to their rightful Lord. Every thought, in the book's phrase, is brought into captivity to Christ. The boy longs to praise God in his life, not only his lips. School, in this telling, is a place of soul-forming. Lessons matter less than conversion.

Evangelical school stories filled Victorian Sunday libraries. They set games and masters inside a frame of faith. A hero's progress was measured in obedience and prayer. Modern readers may find the piety heavy. The book faithfully shows what such schools hoped to make. It is a period piece of religious education.
19907-around-the-world-in-ten-days:
Chelsea Curtis Fraser wrote Around the World in Ten Days as a boys' adventure. Students pour from the Clark Polytechnic Institute doors in its opening. Two boys pause at a newsboy on the street. The taller buys a newspaper and pockets it in his raincoat. From that small start, a dash around the world begins. Ten days for the circuit is the book's daring wager.

Airplanes made Jules Verne's eighty days look slow. Fraser raced his heroes by every fast conveyance of the 1920s. Schoolboys with grit and timetables were his cast. The story teaches geography at running speed. Each stop is a lesson disguised as a deadline. It captures the decade's faith in shrinking distance.
19952-to-the-front-a-sequel-to-cadet-day:
Charles King wrote To the Front as a sequel to Cadet Days, dated 1908. It opens on graduation day at West Point. A remarkable scene marked that morning's ceremonies. The Board of Visitors watched in full attendance. Officers of the academic and military staff stood in full uniform. Something in the ceremony broke its usual order. King, a West Point graduate himself, knew that stage perfectly.

King's cadet stories follow young officers from academy to frontier. Cadet Days made his school reputation; this sequel graduates the class. The front of the title means active service in the Philippines or West. King's soldiers are professionals, not dime-novel heroes. His books taught civilians how the old army worked. Graduation day here is a true threshold scene.
20070-four-days:
Hetty Hemenway published Four Days in 1917, with the subtitle The Story of a War Marriage. The First World War forms the backdrop for a brief, intense tale. One scene fills a station with troops in khaki climbing from train cars. Feet stamp, and young voices shout and call above the roar.

Four days is a short span, and the title stresses that rush. Love and duty must be weighed while war waits for no one. The book shows how war sped up courtship and parting alike. Readers get a home-front tale told at wartime pace and pitch.
20172-the-flutter-of-the-goldleaf-and-ot:
Olive Tilford Dargan wrote The Flutter of the Goldleaf and Other Plays, a set of dramas. One scene shows a wife tidying a room for a New York specialist. Her husband has been too sick to go to the store for days. She dusts and rattles about, keen to hide any trace of disorder.

Plays in this set turn on home life, work, and mountain folk. Dargan wrote of the South and its hills with a poet's ear. Talk in dialect gives her scenes their bite and warmth at once. Readers get period drama where small rooms hold large hopes and fears.
20389-historical-and-political-essays:
William Edward Hartpole Lecky, the Irish historian, gathered these essays from his work for leading reviews. Pieces on Sir Robert Peel, Henry Reeve, and Dean Milman first appeared in the Edinburgh Review. Other essays ran in the Pall Mall Magazine and the Contemporary Review.

The subjects range across politics and letters. One essay treats Queen Victoria as a moral force in the life of the nation. Another, Carlyle's Message to His Age, weighs the prophet-like writer's hold on his times. The book shows Lecky's calm, balanced way of judging public men and public questions.
21187-dr-jolliffe-s-boys:
Weston School's cricket match against Hillsborough opens Lewis Hough's boarding school novel. The crowd roars as their captain Crawley is given out leg before wicket. Life at Doctor Jolliffe's school in the late nineteenth century fills the book. Rules exist mainly to be broken by boys with energy.

The boys slip out of bounds to a forbidden tuck shop and skate near thin ice on a frozen lake. They also poach on a big estate and try cruel country sports like rat baiting. Hough draws each boy's character clearly, scene by scene. Readers wondered why this warm, well-made school story never became better known.
21238-the-castaways:
A ship founders in a typhoon in the Celebes Sea in Captain Mayne Reid's short tale. Her boat brings only a few ashore: the captain, his two children, the Irish ship's carpenter, and the Malay pilot. Two others in the boat die before land is reached. The landing starts a long walk toward Bruni, hundreds of miles away.

Each chapter takes up a plant, tree, or animal of the region. The upas tree, an orangutan, a fruit that drops like a bomb, and a python all appear. The Malay pilot's skill with a blowpipe, which he makes on the spot, saves the party more than once.
21295-cormorant-crag-a-tale-of-the-smugg:
Two boys on a small offshore island off England's south coast anchor George Manville Fenn's tale of the smuggling days around 1830. One is the doctor's son, the other the squire's. Old fisherman Daygo takes them fishing and warns them off one stretch of cliff, where ships that come too close are said to disappear.

Borrowing Daygo's boat, the boys find the truth: a sea cave big enough to hide a small vessel, stocked with fresh smuggled goods. Found inside days later, they are seized by the French smugglers who run the trade. Fenn then works through captures, escapes, and perils that nearly end the boys for good.
21312-glyn-severn-s-schooldays:
Glyn Severn and Singh, the young Maharajah of Dour, are schoolfellows of fifteen or sixteen at an English boarding school in George Manville Fenn's tale. Glyn's father, a colonel in the old Maharajah's army, is now Singh's guardian. A bully named Slegge makes himself their enemy from the start.

A menagerie owner's elephant sometimes turns dangerous, and the two boys, who know elephants from India, prove best at calming it. Then Singh's heavily jewelled princely belt vanishes, and suspicion falls on boys known to be short of money. Half the book hunts the thief, and the surprise ending reaches well beyond the few days of school action.
21452-ernest-bracebridge-school-days:
Ernest Bracebridge stands at the centre of W. H. G. Kingston's school story Ernest Bracebridge. The book opens on a half-holiday, with boys cheering a fellow who has taken his degree as Senior Wrangler. Old faces, old scenes, and warm handshakes set the tone.

Kingston fills the tale with the staff, customs, and small wars of a Victorian school. Ernest is drawn as a near-perfect hero, brave, kind, and steady. A visit to a second school shows how long such customs lived on. Many judges count the book among Kingston's best, and it reads aloud especially well.
21468-marmaduke-merry-a-tale-of-naval-ad:
Marmaduke Merry tells of naval life in bygone days in W. H. G. Kingston's long tale of that name. Action fills the frame, and inside it sailors spin tales of still more action. The manner recalls Captain Marryat, whom Kingston admired and followed.

21688-scottish-cathedrals-and-abbeys:
The Reverend D. Butler surveys Scotland's great churches in Scottish Cathedrals and Abbeys, in the Guild Library. Principal Story writes the introduction to Butler's handbook. Reviewers praised the series for careful workmanship and scholarly industry.

21933-much-darker-days:
Andrew Lang parodies the sensation novel in Much Darker Days, a comic shocker of 1884 issued under the name A. Huge Longway. The title mocks a real bestseller, Dark Days, and Lang's narrator mocks everything else. He confesses to wallowing in crime: stillicide and mayhem are child's play to him. 22279-phil-bradley-s-mountain-boys:
Silas K. Boone wrote Phil Bradley's Mountain Boys, or The Birch Bark Lodge, in 1915. The Mountain Boys series sent Phil and his chums into the woods for their holidays. 22298-practical-mechanics-for-boys:
J. S. Zerbe, a mechanical engineer, wrote Practical Mechanics for Boys to put real shop knowledge into boys' hands. 22334-in-kings-byways:
Stanley J. Weyman wrote In Kings' Byways, a set of tales set around royal courts. The narrator serves in a great lord's household. One morning, he learns that who climbs may fall.

22410-the-crofton-boys:
The Crofton Boys follows a family of children in their London home. Mrs. Proctor takes her children to the Temple Garden each fine evening. There they walk and breathe air from the river.

The boys' lives unfold through home lessons and outings. Period children's books like this taught conduct through example. Readers see siblings learning kindness, patience, and duty in daily rounds. 22675-home-life-in-colonial-days:
Home Life in Colonial Days is Alice Morse Earle's classic study of everyday life in early America. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Earle helped invent the study of colonial daily life, working from houses, inventories, letters, and the objects families actually used.

Her thanks in the preface map her method. Photographers in Boston and Richmond helped, as did the Misses Allen of Deerfield. 22700-brittany-its-byways:
Fanny Bury Palliser wrote Brittany and Its Byways, a travel book through the old province of Brittany in western France. The catalog record gives no year. Palliser, known for works on lace and art, here turns guide, leading readers away from railways into lanes, churches, and fishing towns.

The journey begins with a crossing: a fair wind carried the party in six hours from Poole to Cherbourg. Palliser mixes history, legend, and close description of dress and custom. Her Brittany is the Celtic, devout, sea-bound province that English travelers loved.
22766-electricity-for-boys:
J. S. Zerbe wrote Electricity for Boys, a practical manual that teaches electricity by having boys build the gear themselves. The catalog record gives no year. Zerbe, a mechanical engineer, wrote a shelf of such books, trusting that a boy who winds his own coil understands more than one who only reads rules.

23074-a-voyage-round-the-world-a-book-fo:
A father earns worship in A Voyage Round the World, a book for boys. Other boys might have very good fathers, the young narrator grants, but they were not equal to his. 23234-semiramis-and-other-plays:

Josiah Gilbert Holland wrote Lessons in Life under his pen name, Timothy Titcomb. He had already published Letters to the Young and Gold Foil. A preface thanks readers for their warm welcome of those books.

Holland calls this third venture a work in a kindred field. His familiar essays treat daily conduct, work, and character. He writes in a friendly, direct, moral tone. Victorian families read Titcomb for practical counsel on living well. These essays show his gift for turning common experience into gentle instruction. Titcomb's earlier books sold widely in America and Britain. Plain chapter titles promise advice without academic dress.
literary-and-general-lectures-and-essays:
Charles Kingsley gathers his lectures and essays in this volume. The Stage As It Was Once opens the collection. Thoughts on Shelley and Byron follow among the literary pieces. Alexander Smith, Pope, Tennyson, and Burns receive studies too.

Kingsley praises the ancient stage's reverence for heroic dead. He imagines a future republic recovering that ennobling relaxation. Essays on English composition and sacred art widen the range. Hours with the Mystics and a Maurice memorial close the volume. Poetry of sacred and legendary art receives its own lecture. Frederick Denison Maurice's memorial closes the general essays section.
literary-and-social-essays:
George William Curtis collects his literary and social essays here. Emerson and Hawthorne pieces from 1854 lead the contents. Both first appeared in Homes of American Authors. A North American Review study of Hawthorne's works follows.

Curtis recalls Thackeray in America from Putnam's Magazine, 1853. His Sir Philip Sidney piece stayed unpublished until this collection. Longfellow, Holmes, and Washington Irving receive later essays. The Emerson essay opens in quiet Concord, near Walden Pond. Rachel, the actress, receives an 1855 Putnam's piece here. Concord's spires and Walden's gleam open the Emerson portrait memorably. Putnam's Magazine first printed several of these pieces for Curtis.
little-men-life-at-plumfield-with-jo-s-b:
Louisa May Alcott dedicates this book to Freddy and Johnny. She calls herself their loving Aunt Weedy in the dedication. Chapter One brings ragged Nat to Plumfield's great gate. Mr. Laurence sent him with a letter for the lady.

Contents promise Sundays, patty pans, and a fire brand at school. Naughty Nan, Daisy's ball, and Uncle Teddy vary the terms. Huckleberries, compositions, and crops fill the school year. John Brooke's chapter and Thanksgiving close Jo's boys' story. Composition day and crops show the school's working year. Damon and Pythias retell friendship among Jo's boys.
lyra-heroica-a-book-of-verse-for-boys:
Lyra Heroica is a book of heroic verse for boys, chosen by William Ernest Henley. Scribner's held the copyright from 1891, and this text follows their 1920 printing. A line from Scott sounds the keynote: one crowded hour of glorious life. The poems begin with Shakespeare and Drayton on Agincourt.

Henley gathered battle songs, ballads, and stirring lyrics of many ages. Whitman, Longfellow, Lowell, Whittier, and Bret Harte all appear here. The book aims to fire boys with tales of courage and honor. Its editor was himself a poet of fighting spirit. Generations of schoolboys met great poetry first in these pages. It remains a rousing shelf of English and American verse.
maezli-a-story-of-the-swiss-valleys:
Maezli is a story of the Swiss valleys by Johanna Spyri. Elisabeth P. Stork translated it, and this edition dates from 1921. Spyri also wrote Heidi and Cornelli, the beloved children's tales. The scene is the village of Nolla, near Castle Wildenstein.

Little Maezli shouts for the castle steward with a child's boldness. Her brother Lippo studies a strange performance with care. An unexpected apparition at the castle stirs the village. New friends, a mother's absence, and visits fill the chapters. Spyri writes of Alpine children with warmth and faith. Maezli's sunny spirit holds the small story together. It is a gentle companion to Heidi.
memories-of-childhood-s-slavery-days:
Annie L. Burton published this memoir in Boston in 1909. She looks back on her childhood as an enslaved girl on a Southern plantation. The Civil War was raging around her, yet she remembers those years as happy and carefree. Her account preserves a child's view of slavery from inside it.

Burton describes days spent roaming with ten white and fourteen Black children. She tells how enslaved workers received weekly allowances of molasses, meat, and corn meal. She also recalls stolen hogs, the whipping post, and an overseer who did the punishing. Her plain, warm memories sit beside these hard facts, and that contrast gives the book its power.
miscellaneous-essays:
Thomas De Quincey's publishers planned this volume as the third in a uniform set of his writings. The essays range across literature, murder, history, and travel. The collection opens with On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth. De Quincey says that knocking puzzled him from boyhood, reflecting an awful solemnity back on Duncan's murder.

Murder, Considered as One of the Fine Arts gives the volume its most famous title. A second paper on murder follows, beside Joan of Arc and The English Mail-Coach. The Vision of Sudden Death and a piece on dinners round out the set. Few essayists mixed confession, criticism, and dark comedy like De Quincey.
miscellaneous-studies-a-series-of-essays: Walter Horatio Pater published Miscellaneous Studies as a series of essays, and the catalog lists the work under that simple description. Pater was the leading English art critic of his generation, known for his studies of the Renaissance. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the book itself. It contains only the Project Gutenberg header, with the title, author's name, and release data. Readers therefore get the volume's identity, but the sample offers none of its essays or arguments.
mr-dooley-says:
Charles Scribner's Sons published this later collection of Finley Peter Dunne's Dooley monologues. The contents list twenty topics for the bartender-philosopher. Divorce, glory, and woman suffrage open the volume. A bachelor tax, panics, and ocean travel follow. Work, drugs, and a broken friendship receive their chapters.

Later pieces take up the tariff, expert testimony, and the Japanese scare. The Hague Conference and Turkish politics close the list. Mr. Dooley, of Archey Road in Chicago, pronounces on each subject for his silent friend Hennessy. By this volume, Dunne's creation was an institution: America's favorite fictional commentator on public life.
mrs-general-talboys:
Anthony Trollope tells this short tale from his Tales of All Countries, printed in 1864. Mrs. General Talboys comes to Rome for the winter of 1859. She tells friends she seeks classical poetry and feeling. The narrator doubts that is the whole truth.

He hints at a spat of temper back home in Berkshire. The General is hot, and his wife can be hard to please. Among the English in Rome she soon finds a firm place. Trollope watches her charm, pride, and push with dry humor. The tale is a neat sketch of a strong woman abroad among her own kind.
my-young-days:
An unnamed author wrote this children's book, issued in New York in 1872. Dutton published it, with Seeley, Jackson and Halliday in London. Paul Konewka drew its twenty pictures. The author had written Evening Amusement and Letters Everywhere.

Chapters move from homesickness to Uncle Hugh's story and a little stowaway. Lessons, holidays, and a cottage on the cliff follow. Susette's troubles and autumn days fill the middle. The book ends with goodbye to Beecham. It is a gentle Victorian tale of home, cousins, and school days, told for young readers in short, warm chapters.
nan-sherwood-s-winter-holidays-or-rescui:
Annie Roe Carr published this Nan Sherwood tale in 1916. It opens on Pendragon Hill above frozen Lake Huron. Professor Krenner blows a silver bugle across the ice. The girls of Lakeview Hall are out for winter sports.

Near Christmas, the shore and strait lie locked in solid ice. A bobsled course runs down the hill to the Isle of Hope. The castle-like Hall shows its roof above the trees. Runaways need rescuing, as the title promises. Carr mixes skating, sledding, and schoolgirl pluck in a bright holiday adventure for her young readers.
nasa-tm-19650009356-ibm-1401-selective-t:
Patricia Ann Savage, in the Data Systems Division at Goddard, wrote this August 1964 program manual. It describes an IBM 1401 computer program that copies selected data from tape to punched cards. The manual belongs to the AOPB systems series, for advanced orbital programming work.

Savage sets out the program objective first, then its description. Manuals like this one told operators and programmers exactly what a program did. In 1964, tape and cards were normal ways to move data between machines. The manual preserves how Goddard handled that routine but vital step. It also shows the division of labor behind orbital work, where small support programs kept larger missions supplied with usable data.
nasa-tm-19650021951-composition-of-solar:
S Biswas, of the Tata Institute in Bombay, and C E Fichtel, of Goddard, wrote this study of what solar cosmic rays are made of. During major solar disturbances, the Sun speeds particles to high energies. Forbush first realized this in 1946 from ground-level observations. Such events grow more common in years of high solar activity, the authors note.

Knowing the mix of particles matters for both science and safety. Different particles carry different energy and do different harm. The authors review evidence from several experiments on event composition. Their study helps explain how the Sun accelerates matter, and what arrives at Earth when a big event occurs.
nasa-tm-19660004934-a-study-of-the-jpl-m:
Mark I ranging gear, built by the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, is studied in this report from the Deep Space Instrumentation Facility. Ranging tells how far away a spacecraft is, by timing a radio signal's round trip. The Mark I was a special version of the MOD II ranging equipment, the catalog note says. Deep space missions depend on such measures for navigation.

A study of the subsystem records its design and behavior for its users. Precise range fixes the spacecraft's path between planets. Errors there grow into missed targets over long flights. Engineers planning later ranging gear needed a clear account of what the Mark I did well.
nasa-tm-19660014184-surface-treatments-f:
Manley W Mallett prepared this October 1965 study of surface treatments for titanium alloys, under the Redstone Scientific Information Center for the Army Missile Command. A treatment changes only a metal's outer skin. It can harden the surface, protect it from attack, or prepare it for coating. Metal coating processes for titanium are the focus named in the catalog note.

Titanium's surface resists many treatments that work on steel. Its own tough oxide forms at once in air. Knowing which processes truly work saves failed parts and wasted trials. Mallett gathers those processes in one reference for shops and designers. Missile work at Redstone Arsenal gave the study its immediate users and its practical tone.
nasa-tm-19660020103-the-lunar-orbiter-te:
W T Bundick, C H Green, and E A Brummer at Langley described the radio system of the Lunar Orbiter in a paper given in Miami Beach in November 1965. Lunar Orbiter was an uncrewed satellite sent to photograph the Moon. It would take high-resolution pictures of wide areas, the authors say. Its tracking approach followed the pattern already used for Ranger and other deep space craft.

Telemetry and tracking during launch ran through the Eastern Test Range, the paper states. Afterward, deep space stations took over the link. Photographs are worthless until they reach Earth, so the telecommunication system was mission-critical. The paper covers both the spacecraft gear and the ground equipment as one designed whole.
nasa-tm-19660020678-solar-modulation-of-:
A Goddard report dated May 1966, numbered X-611-66-226, studies how the Sun changes the cosmic rays that reach Earth from the galaxy. Galactic cosmic rays are fast particles from deep space. As they cross the solar system, the solar wind and its field weaken and scatter them. That change is called solar modulation. Protons and helium nuclei are the particles named in the catalog note.

The ratio between protons and helium nuclei helps reveal how the change works. Each kind of particle answers the solar wind in its own way. Tracking the ratio over time ties cosmic ray readings to solar activity. Such work served both space weather studies and the design of shielding for crewed flight.
nasa-tm-19700026432-manual-booster-contr:
Manual control of a booster rocket gets a dispersion analysis in this Houston internal note, number MSC-CF-P-69-22. Dispersion means the spread of flight paths that small errors can cause when a crew steers by hand. The note backs contingency procedures that let astronauts fly a Saturn themselves if automatic steering failed.

The procedures were checked in the Dynamic Crew Procedures Simulator, in launch and translunar injection phases. Six test subjects flew the runs to give a cross section of pilot performance, and two had current mission assignments. Crews steered by comparing actual attitude, speed, and height against cue card values. The data, the note states, show crew control is feasible within acceptable limits.
nasa-tm-19700031003-techniques-for-gamma:
Carl E. Fichtel of the Goddard Space Flight Center gave this invited talk in Munich, Germany, in August 1970. The occasion was a symposium on new techniques in space astronomy. His subject is gamma rays, the most energetic kind of light arriving from space, and the instruments built to catch them.

Gamma ray study is a young field, Fichtel explains, because air blocks these photons low down. Detectors must ride high altitude balloons or small satellites above most of the atmosphere. He reviews the kinds of instruments flown in the past and what each design could measure. The talk then turns to instruments planned for future flights or still being proposed.
nasa-tm-19700032772-stability-of-a-two-d:
Mitchell Cash of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on July 24, 1970. It studies the stability of a simple column model that can move in two ways. The column faces both steady loads and sudden blows, called impulsive loads.

Cash uses energy methods to judge when the model will collapse. A soft spring in the model is what makes collapse possible. He allows for small flaws in the starting shape of the column. The study finds how much extra starting energy collapse takes under each condition. Computer runs then show how the model answers over time, and how each factor changes that answer.
nasa-tm-19710007230-compound-diffusion-o:
R. E. Lingenfelter, R. Ramaty, and L. A. Fisk of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in January 1971. It treats compound diffusion of cosmic rays. Cosmic rays are fast particles that cross space and strike Earth's upper air, arriving almost evenly from every direction.

That evenness, called low anisotropy, is the paper's starting clue about how the rays travel. If the rays moved only along tidy, uniform magnetic field lines, a lopsided arrival pattern would be as likely as an even one. Our even sky would then be a mere accident of where and when we sit. Against that picture, the authors set much evidence that the interstellar field is disordered on smaller scales.
nasa-tm-19720012196-mechanical-design-of:
Ralph J Zavesky and Evert B Hurst of the Lewis Research Center described this ion thruster design in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2518. The mercury bombardment thruster flew on the SERT 2 spacecraft. SERT 2 carried two such thrusters into orbit. The report shows how many design pressures shaped one machine. Structure, heat, wiring, and material choices all pulled on the final design, as did stray mercury coatings.

SERT 2 launched on February 3, 1970. One thruster ran for about thirty seven hundred hours in orbit. The other ran for about two thousand hours. A high voltage short finally stopped the test. Loose eroded material building up inside was blamed for the short.
nine-short-essays:
Charles Dudley Warner gathered Nine Short Essays in this small book. Titles include A Night in the Garden of the Tuileries, Truthfulness, and The Pursuit of Happiness. Literature and the Stage, Simplicity, and Nathan Hale also appear. One piece visits H. H. in Southern California.

The Tuileries essay opens in Paris under the Second Empire, on June 18, 1868. Warner calls it the longest night he ever saw, in the loveliest time of year. By day the garden held idle Paris sunning itself, children chasing butterflies, and bands playing. By night some new pleasure always led the hours along. Warner's essays move easily between travel, morals, and books.
old-caravan-days:
Mary Hartwell Catherwood wrote this pioneer story for young readers. The contents follow a wagon journey in early America. Chapters name a tavern, a camp meeting, and a darkened wagon. A child hears a cry in the night. Fairies, minstrels, and settlers all enter the tale.

Catherwood shows the hard, hopeful life of moving west. Families face hunger, fear, and strange new neighbors. Warm scenes balance danger on the road. The story keeps the feel of old caravan travel alive. Later heads name the Susan House and its cellar rooms. A house with log steps stands near the close.
old-indian-days:
Charles Eastman, also called Ohiyesa, wrote these Sioux stories. He dedicated the book to his five daughters. The contents split into two parts, warrior and woman. Warrior tales name Antelope, Bald Eagle, and a famine. Woman tales follow Winona, Snana, and a war maiden.

Eastman recalls the old Indian life before reservations. Stories stress courage, loyalty, and women's strength. A glossary helps readers with Dakota words and names. The book preserves memory from inside the culture. It remains a valued firsthand record of Sioux life. Part one also names the Singing Spirit and the Chief Soldier. Part two adds the Peace-Maker and Blue Sky tales.
oldport-days:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson wrote these sketches of Oldport. Lee and Shepard published the book in Boston in 1888. The copyright dates to 1873 under another publisher. Contents include Oldport in winter and Oldport wharves. Other pieces treat a haunted window and driftwood fires.

Higginson describes summer crowds rushing through the resort town. In September the great hotels close and calm returns. Sailors, gossips, and quiet streets fill the sketches. His fond tone keeps a lost New England alive. The book is a small classic of town life. The list adds a wherry trip and Madam Delia's hopes. Bronze dogs once guarded the Ocean House doors, Higginson notes.
ostrovsky-plays:
Merchant Moscow comes alive in the Plays of Alexander Ostrovsky, presented here in English. Tyrannical fathers, scheming traders, clever clerks, and suffering women fill his famous dark kingdom of the counting-house and the family firm. Ostrovsky dominated the Russian stage for half a century, writing the merchant class into literature almost single-handedly.

His dialogue catches the speech of the Zamoskvorechye district, proverb-rich and status-obsessed. Plots turn on dowries, debts, and marriages arranged like contracts, until feeling breaks the ledger open. These translations open his world to English readers who know Russian drama mainly through Chekhov. Ostrovsky is the foundation Chekhov built on. The plays still hold the stage in Russia season after season.
outspoken-essays: William Ralph Inge, dean of St. Paul's Cathedral, gathered his Outspoken Essays in 1920. Inge was famous for saying exactly what he thought in print. He was often denounced for it too. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. Our Present Discontents, Patriotism, and The Birth-Rate are promised. Cardinal Newman and Saint Paul follow. Survival and Immortality closes the volume. No essay text appears.
patty-s-butterfly-days: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Patty's Butterfly Days, the title page and table of contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Carolyn Wells, author of the Patty and Marjorie books, and Martin Lewis as illustrator. The contents list a dinner party, a garden party, a house party, a drive and a bad storm, pageant plans, and chapters named for Aunt Adelaide and Big Bill Farnsworth.
peck-s-bad-boy-with-the-cowboys: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Peck's Bad Boy with the Cowboys, the title pages and list of illustrations, with no chapter text visible. The title page names George W. Peck and describes the amusing experiences of the Bad Boy and his pa among cowboys and Indians in the Far West, with hunts and adventures promised. The copyright pages run from 1905 to 1907, and the frontispiece shows the pair asking, "Got any trailing dogs?"
peter-plymley-s-letters-and-selected-ess:
Sydney Smith's Peter Plymley's Letters, and Selected Essays appears here in Cassell's National Library, from the 1893 edition. A long introduction tells Smith's life: born at Woodford in 1771, of partly French descent, schooled at Winchester and New College, Oxford. Against his own wish he took orders and became curate of Netherhaven in Wiltshire, where meat arrived once a week.

The Peter Plymley letters, written under that mask, argued for Catholic emancipation with wit that made them famous. The selected essays show the other Smith: clergyman, Edinburgh Review founder, and the funniest talker of his age.
plays:
Susan Glaspell's Plays gathers four works by the American writer: Trifles, The Outside, The Verge, and Inheritors. Trifles, the best known of the set, was first staged by the Provincetown Players at the Wharf Theatre on August 8, 1916.

Trifles opens in the gloomy kitchen of an abandoned farmhouse, the home of John Wright. A sheriff, a county attorney, and a farmer search the house while their wives wait by the stove. The cast list names Mrs. Peters and Mrs. Hale, and the scene is set with unwashed pans and work left half done.
podcast-dannyjones-5H2Wbnosgys:
Astrophysicist Brian Keating takes the skeptical chair on Danny Jones's podcast, explaining why scientists like him are highly doubtful of UFO whistleblower David Grusch and the disclosure movement built around his claims. Keating argues that extraordinary claims have so far arrived without extraordinary evidence.

Keating's standard is the laboratory one: data that others can check. Jones, whose show usually platforms the believers, lets the critic make his case at length, and the contrast is the point. The episode gives listeners the strongest mainstream answer to the claims heard across this series. For anyone trying to judge the UFO debate fairly, hearing a respected physicist explain exactly what would convince him, and why nothing yet has, is essential balance.
podcast-joerogan-Fih4cYdsoYs:
Skeptic Michael Shermer joins Joe Rogan to talk UFO events in a segment from the show. Shermer is a famed debunker who runs a magazine for doubt. He comes to the lore with a cold eye and a list of past frauds.

Shermer walks through famed cases and shows where the proof thins out. He grants what he cannot explain and holds the line on the rest. Rogan, who loves the lore, trades tales with him in good sport. Listeners get the doubt side in a strong voice. The library holds the segment as an archive record of the debate.
podcast-joerogan-hxKR6gtkSYs:
Thoughts is the title of an excerpt from episode 543 of the Joe Rogan Experience, built around Sam Harris. Harris, the philosopher, was by then a regular sparring partner for Rogan. The excerpt keeps their early, sharp exchanges in one place.

The two work over the mind, morals, and meditation, subjects Harris would soon make into books and an app. Rogan answers from instinct, Harris from argument, and the gaps between them are the interest. The excerpt is early gold from the show's vault, a sample of the pairing before their later, tenser years, when the respect was still easy.
podcast-joerogan-mBjGLZww8Ys:
Joe Rogan trades near-death stories under the title Buried in Snow. The clip gathers tales of close calls in wild places. Rogan often returns to fear, luck, and survival on his show.

One story starts on a Hawaii beach with rough surf. A swimmer recalls telling himself not to panic as waves hit. Other tales deal with cold, snow, and bad choices outdoors. The talk shows how fast a fun trip can turn grave. It suits listeners who like true survival stories told in a raw, first-person way. A clear theme emerges: calm minds survive, panic kills.
practical-essays:
Alexander Bain, emeritus professor of logic at the University of Aberdeen, collected his Practical Essays in London in 1884, mostly reprinting articles from the reviews. Bain, the Scottish philosopher who completed the associationist psychology of the Mills. Admits in his preface that the practical character of the pieces is their only real bond, apart from his own individuality and range of studies. Novelty, he promises, will be found on the most cursory perusal.

Two essays apply the laws of mind to prevailing errors. Two more take up education, the subjects proper for competitive examinations and the vexed classical controversy. Others treat metaphysical study in debating societies, the growth of the universities and the university ideal beyond professional teaching. A chapter from his Science of Education on self-education by books. Bain at his most useful is a Victorian sage giving instructions for thinking and studying in the real world.
quadrupeds-what-they-are-and-where-found:
Quadrupeds, What They Are and Where Found is a book of zoology for boys by Captain Mayne Reid, dated 1885. Reid wrote the sketches to go with a set of engravings, sorting the mammals into twenty-four groups and stressing where each animal lives rather than strict science.

His preface calls the sketches popular, with Latin names kept out, and hopes they will start a young reader toward a better sorting of the mammals than any yet made. Chapter one takes the monkeys of the Old World. It treats the orang-outang of Borneo and Sumatra. It treats the chimpanzee of West Africa. The long-armed gibbons come next. The proboscis monkeys of Borneo follow.
quotations-from-diary-of-samuel-pepys: Quotations from the Diary of Samuel Pepys is number 17 in the Widger's Quotations series, prepared by David Widger. The pages shown are the Project Gutenberg header alone. The header gives the title. It names Widger as author. It dates the file's first posting to November 28, 2001. The release date is July 2003. It prints the standard license and donation notices. No quotations from the diary itself appear on these opening pages.
quotes-and-images-from-the-diary-of-samu:
Quotes and Images from the Diary of Pepys, prepared by David Widger, mines Samuel Pepys's diary for short, vivid entries and sets them in alphabetical order. Unlike the bare Widger's Quotations header volume of the same diary, this selection gives the extracts themselves, page after page.

Pepys kisses a good handsome wench, the first he has seen. He calls one man most conceited. He calls another tedious in a sermon. He notes twenty shillings and wine allowed for a burial. A lady spits backward on him by mistake, a play is not very good though much commended, and an act of council orders all Papists out of office.
read-aloud-plays: Read-Aloud Plays, by Horace Holley, was published in New York by Mitchell Kennerley in 1916, with dramatic and lecture rights reserved by the author. Only the title pages and contents are shown. After an introduction come nine short plays: Her Happiness, A Modern Prodigal, The Incompatibles, The Genius, Survival, The Telegram, Rain, Pictures, and His Luck, the last beginning at page 121.
redemption-and-two-other-plays:
Leo Tolstoy's plays are gathered here under the names Fruits of Culture and Redemption, and the cast list of Redemption fills the opening pages. Its people center on Theodore Vasilyevich Protosov, called Fédya, and his wife Lisa, with their son Misha. Lisa's mother and her younger sister Sasha stand near them.

Victor Karénin loves Lisa, and Prince Sergius Abréskov and the gypsy girl Masha widen the circle. Gypsy singers, waiters, a policeman, and an investigating magistrate crowd the later list. Boon companions, an artist, and a young lawyer complete a cast shaped for a drama of marriage, drink, and ruin in Russian society.
revolution-and-other-essays:
Jack London argues for revolution in the title essay of this set, issued by Mills and Boon of London in 1910. A saying of Huxley heads the book: new truths begin as heresies and end as superstitions. The title essay opens with a letter from a man in Arizona, signed Yours for the Revolution.

London says some four hundred thousand men, and nearly a million men and women, in the United States sign letters Dear Comrade in the same cause. Other essays treat The Somnambulists, The Dignity of Dollars, and The Shrinkage of the Planet. The Yellow Peril, The Gold Hunters of the North, and What Life Means to Me close the list.
rides-on-railways:
Samuel Sidney wrote this railway companion for travellers who care little where they go, so long as the journey instructs. His preface is dated from London in August 1851. The book aims to amuse and inform riders bound for Wales, the Lakes of Cumberland, or the Highlands of Scotland, and to show them the towns they pass.

Sidney promises manufactures, mines, and the sources of the island's commerce as well as rural scenes. He drew on his own watching, on notes and memory of former journeys, and on cyclopaedias and local guide-books. The contents open on the London and North Western Railway: Euston Station, the mixed train, Camden, Aylesbury, and Oxford.
round-the-world-in-seven-days: Herbert Strang wrote Round the World in Seven Days, with pictures by A. C. Michael, dated 1910. The contents list a prelude, an interlude, and chapters that race eastward round the globe. Early titles include The Cablegram, Eastward Ho, Across Europe to the Bosphorus, A Flying Visit, and The Tomb of Ur-Gur. Later chapters turn to gun runners in the Gulf, The White Djinn, A Ship on Fire, A Passenger for Penang, Some Praus and a Junk, and Australian Hospitality.
sanitary-and-social-lectures-and-essays:
Charles Kingsley wrote Sanitary and Social Lectures and Essays, transcribed from the 1880 Macmillan edition in London. The contents list eleven pieces, opening with Woman's Work in a Country Parish, The Science of Health, and The Two Breaths. Later titles include Thrift, Nausicaa in London, or the Lower Education of Women, The Air-Mothers, The Tree of Knowledge, and Great Cities and Their Influence for Good and Evil. The list closes with Heroism, The Massacre of the Innocents, and A Mad World, My Masters.

The first lecture, on a lady's work in a country parish, opens with Kingsley's method. Asked to speak a few words on the subject, he says he will confine himself to principles rather than details. The first principle he would impress is that people must all be just before they are generous.
schnitzler-the-lonely-way-intermezzo-cou:
Three plays by Arthur Schnitzler share this English volume: The Lonely Way, Intermezzo, and Countess Mizzi. Artists, lovers, and the Viennese upper classes navigate love, aging, and self-deception across all three. A dying poet, an estranged theatrical couple, and an aging countess anchor the separate plots.

Witty dialogue plays over abysses of feeling, the trademark Schnitzler balance. Old flames return; parents and children misread each other; success proves a lonely address. Together the plays show the dramatist at his most characteristic in English dress. Readers who know the Reigen will find a broader, tenderer range here. The volume suits an evening's reading that lingers for weeks afterward.
science-education-essays:
Thomas H. Huxley collected his talks on schooling in Science and Education Essays, writing the preface at Hodeslea, Eastbourne, on September 4, 1893. He warns readers that pieces on one theme, given across thirty years, will repeat themselves. The talks went to very different crowds in distant places, so some overlap could not be helped.

Huxley points to his earliest piece, an 1854 talk on the teaching worth of natural history, as rough work he later disowned in part. Still, he says, his later views mostly grow from claims first stated there. The list of pieces runs from a life of Joseph Priestley to talks on liberal schooling and on emancipation. One late essay bears on fights over teaching religion in board schools.
second-plays:
A. A. Milne gathered five stage pieces in this companion volume to his First Plays, issued in New York by Alfred A. Knopf. Milne had already published verse, essays, and the novel Mr. Pim. The contents list Make-Believe, Mr. Pim Passes By, The Camberley Triangle, The Romantic Age, and The Stepmother.

Make-Believe, a play for children in a prologue and three acts, opened at the Lyric Theatre, Hammersmith, on December 24, 1918. One cast of ten actors filled many parts each. Light wit and neat reversals mark the set, which shows Milne's stage craft before his fame as a writer for children grew.
shakespeare-and-the-modern-stage-with-ot:
Sidney Lee, author of a life of William Shakespeare, published these essays with Archibald Constable in London in 1907. The lead essay attacks showy modern staging of the plays. Lee lists perils of the spectacular method and urges simpler scenery in its place.

Lee weighs what Charles Kean and Henry Irving spent on staging, and praises Samuel Phelps's leaner trials. He argues that the actor should rule the stage, as on French and German boards. Shakespeare, he holds, trusted the crowd's power to imagine. Other essays round out a critic's case for plain, actor-led production.
six-plays:
Florence Henrietta Darwin wrote these six country plays, issued by W. Heffer and Sons at Cambridge in 1921 with an opening essay by Cecil Sharp. Titles include Lovers' Tasks, Bushes and Briars, My Man John, and The Seeds of Love. The plays sold in paper covers at one shilling and sixpence.

Sharp states his sympathy plainly: the work aims to restore the English peasant to his rightful estate on stage. Sharp's own twenty years among country folk ground his praise. Village speech, courtship, and seasonal custom fill plays built for local acting and for readers who valued rural England's fast-fading ways.
six-short-plays:
John Galsworthy wrote these six short plays, opening with The First and the Last. That drama, in three scenes, sets brothers Keith and Larry Darrant against each other, with Wanda between them. Keith's study at six on a November evening opens the action: dark curtains, a reading lamp, and a log fire.

Keith, a leading lawyer in red Turkish slippers and a brown velvet coat, sleeps in his armchair. Larry slips in so softly through the curtained door that Keith does not wake. Other plays here include The Little Man, Hall-Marked, Defeat, The Sun, and Punch and Go.
some-turns-of-thought-in-modern-philosop: George Santayana groups five essays in Some Turns of Thought in Modern Philosophy. Charles Scribner's Sons printed the book at New York in 1933. The Royal Society of Literature backed the issue. The contents open with Locke and the Frontiers of Common Sense. Santayana read that paper for the three-hundredth year of Locke's birth. Fifty Years of British Idealism comes next. A new printing of Bradley's Ethical Studies sparked it. Revolutions in Science follows. A Long Way Round to Nirvana comes fourth. The Prestige of the Infinite closes the set.
spring-days:
George Moore looks back on the fate of his novel Spring Days in a long preface. When Henry Vizetelly was sent to prison for printing Zola's novels, Moore's books were taken over by Walter Scott, and all were reprinted save Spring Days. The book was left off his owned list, for public and private judgment had shown it no mercy, and he had lost faith in it.

All the welcome it got, he says, was a few scornful paragraphs in the press and one rude piece in The Academy. He took care not to see that piece. Worse, he had given the book to the editor of a great London review after a night of talk and quotes from Greek, English, and Latin classics. The editor never owned the copy sent him, not even through a clerk. Moore bore the snub without spite and put his trust in time.
the-atlantic-book-of-modern-plays: Front matter and a partial contents list present The Atlantic Book of Modern Plays. Sterling Andrus Leonard of the University of Wisconsin edited it. The Atlantic Monthly Press of Boston printed it in 1921. Leonard supplies an introduction, comments, and a noted book list. A notice warns that staging rights stay with each author. Reading in classrooms and free school shows are still allowed. The contents open with an essay on reading plays. They list Harold Chapin's The Philosopher of Butterbiggens and Lady Gregory's Spreading the News.
the-birth-time-of-the-world-and-other-sc:
J. Joly, professor of geology and mineralogy at the University of Dublin, gathered scientific essays under a title about the world's birth-time. E. P. Dutton published the volume in New York. A frontispiece shows the Lake of Lucerne looking west from Brunnen.

Contents start with the title essay at page one, then denudation, the abundance of life, and bright colours of alpine flowers. Mountain genesis and alpine structure follow. Later essays treat other minds than ours, the latent image, pleochroic haloes, radium in medicine, and skating. A final speculation concerns a pre-material universe, joining earth science with physics and natural history.
the-castaways:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this sea adventure, dated 1870 in its heading. Seven people drift in an open boat on a tropical sea, with no sail, no mast, and no land in sight. One of the seven is already dead. The living include a tall New Yorker, a red-haired Irishman, a worn sailor, a Malay man, and a brother and sister in their teens.

The opening chapter sorts the cast one by one, face by face, so readers know each person before the struggle starts. Hunger, sun, and still water press on the group from the first pages. Reid builds the tale as a survival story, where small choices about food, water, and hope carry weight. Readers who like plain, close detail about life at sea will find the boat itself treated almost like a character.
the-diary-of-samuel-pepys: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands at the head of this record for The Diary of Samuel Pepys. The header carries the project's old-style copyright warnings, its plea for donations, and the foundation's Oxford, Mississippi address, before closing title and author lines name the work and Samuel Pepys. No contents, preface, or diary entry follows in what is present here.
the-function-of-the-poet-and-other-essay:
James Russell Lowell wrote the essays in The Function of the Poet, gathered and edited by Albert Mordell from pieces in the Century Magazine of 1893 and 1894. A note by Charles Eliot Norton stands with the title essay.

Lowell writes on the poet's task, on humor, wit, fun, and satire, and on the five authors no reader can skip: Homer, Dante, Cervantes, Goethe, and Shakespeare. He adds pieces on the imagination and on style and manner, then reviews of his peers. Mordell's letter at the front is dated January 13, 1920. The book keeps a great American critic's late, ripe thought on books and men.
the-gorgon-s-head-from-a-wonder-book-for:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Gorgon's Head. It is part of A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys. The contents frame the tale with a Tanglewood Porch introduction. A further Tanglewood Porch piece follows the story. In his preface Hawthorne states a long-held view. Many classical myths, he says, could be made into fine reading for children.

He worked up half a dozen myths with that end in view. He took great freedom in the telling. The old legends, he argues, stay the same under changes that would undo almost anything else. No age can claim a copyright in these fables. They seem never to have been made. They can never perish while man exists. Each age may clothe them in its own manners and morals. The Gorgon's Head retells the Perseus myth on those terms. It is shaped for young readers.
the-house-of-the-combrays:
G. Le Notre wrote this French history. Mrs. Joseph B. Gilder translated it into English. Dodd, Mead and Company published it in New York in 1902. The narrative opens as a story told after dinner. The winter was 1868 or 1869. The narrator's father-in-law, Moisson, picks up a novel. He reveals that he knew its heroine. Her real name was Mme. de Combray. He once lived three months in her house.

Moisson corrects the novel as he goes. The real woman lived at her château near Gaillon. She was no saintly heroine. From that fireside correction the book unfolds. It tells of the Combrays and the Chouan rebels. Those royalists fought the French Revolution in the west. Family memory mixes with documented history throughout.
the-humour-of-homer-and-other-essays:
Samuel Butler's essays receive a new frame in this edition. R. A. Streatfeild prepared it. The core is a collection from 1904. Grant Richards published it as Essays on Life, Art and Science. A reissue followed in 1908. This edition adds the title essay. It also adds a life sketch by Henry Festing Jones. A photogravure portrait from 1889 appears. The Humour of Homer began as a lecture. Butler delivered it at the Working Men's College. The date was January 30, 1892.

That date matters in Butler's story. The same day, he announced his Homer theory in print. He argued the Odyssey came from Trapani in Sicily. Five years of research followed. The result was The Authoress of the Odyssey in 1897. Streatfeild presents the lecture as a lively introduction. Part of it, on the Iliad, never entered the later book. That section alone makes the lecture worth knowing.
the-kellys-and-the-o-kellys: Anthony Trollope published this Irish novel in 1848, subtitled Landlords and Tenants. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. Thirty-nine chapter headings sketch two linked courtships and a lawsuit. The trial and the two heiresses open them. Morrison's Hotel and a morning call by Barry Lynch follow. Martin Kelly's courtship and Anty Lynch's bedside come next. Lord Ballindine at home and the hunt appear. Fanny Wyndham rebels midway. A countess in trouble closes the arc.
the-log-of-a-cowboy-a-narrative-of-the-o: Andy Adams wrote The Log of a Cowboy, subtitled A Narrative of the Old Trail Days. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published it in Boston and New York in 1903, with illustrations by E. Boyd Smith. Only the title page and part of the contents are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear. Chapters shown include Up the Trail, Receiving, The Start, The Atascosa, A Dry Drive, A Reminiscent Night, The Colorado, and Doan's Crossing. Adams dedicated the book to the cowmen and boys of the old western trail.
the-master-key-an-electrical-fairy-tale-:
L. Frank Baum subtitled The Master Key an electrical fairy tale, founded on the mysteries of electricity and the optimism of its devotees. Baum says he wrote it for boys, though others may read it. The hero, Rob, keeps a workshop where he experiments with electrical devices. His tinkering brings him face to face with the Demon of Electricity, who grants him three gifts.

The contents promise tests of the instruments, a cannibal island, buccaneers, and service to a mighty king. Rob saves a republic, loses his treasures, battles monsters, and survives shipwreck on his journeys. A short opening meditation asks whether today's impossibilities become tomorrow's accepted facts. Baum frames Rob's wonders as playful prophecy about coming technology. Young readers get adventure built from the newest science of Baum's day, when electricity still seemed half magic.
the-miraculous-pitcher-from-a-wonder-boo:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's story The Miraculous Pitcher comes from A Wonder-Book for Girls and Boys, his retelling of Greek myths for children. The frame opens in May, with the Tanglewood children climbing a great hill behind their storyteller, Cousin Eustace. Eustace, home for spring vacation, sports the funniest little bit of a mustache on his upper lip. He carries the smaller children, Dandelion, Cowslip, and Squash-blossom, up the steep ascent in turn.

The party passes orchards and pastures and reaches the wood below the hill's bald summit. Violets, blue and white and golden, crowd their path on a sweet, genial day. Hawthorne's frame promises the myth itself next, followed by a closing scene back on the hillside. The Greek tale behind the title, of kindness rewarded by an ever-flowing pitcher, is retold for young listeners at a picnic's pace.
the-playboy-of-the-western-world-and-oth: The Playboy of the Western World and Other Plays collects plays by J. M. Synge in a Signet Classics printing issued at New York in 1997. Here only the front matter of that modern edition appears, so the plays themselves are absent. The contents list two one-act plays, In the Shadow of the Glen and Riders to the Sea. The title play in three acts follows, plus an afterword. Notes give Synge's dates, 1871 to 1909, his Trinity studies, and Yeats's advice to live among the people of the Aran Islands.
the-rhythm-of-life-and-other-essays:
Alice Meynell's essays, transcribed from a John Lane edition of 1893, begin with a claim that life, if not always poetical, is at least metrical. Periodicity rules mental experience, she argues, as thoughts return along their orbits without our measuring distances or times.

Happiness depends on tides of the mind rather than events, and disease itself arrives metrically, closing toward death or widening toward recovery. Companion essays treat the sun, flowers, landscape, caricature, and writers including Holmes, Lowell, and Patmore. The collection rewards readers who like short prose built on rhythm and recurrence.
the-spectator-volume-1-eighteenth-centur: Henry Morley, professor of English literature at University College, London, edited this new edition of The Spectator. It runs to three volumes, dated 1891. The edition reproduces the original text both as first issued and as corrected by its authors, with introduction, notes, and index. The pages present here for volume one carry the title page and a publisher's advertisement. The advertisement offers editions of Shakespeare, Boswell, Byron, and others, and a stretch of verse follows, so the essays of the volume itself do not appear.
the-spirit-of-place-and-other-essays:
Seventeen short essays, transcribed from a 1899 John Lane edition, range over solitude, rain, sleep, and the horizon. They also treat habits of consciousness, with no author's name printed on the pages present here. The title essay opens with bells, complaining that poets have all but outsung them with mimicry, praise, and echoes.

The essayist notes that people do bells actual violence. They force grim wedding bells to seem gay by mere hustling. A clock plays less arbitrarily, and its chimes fly free at their appointed time. Hours of the past, once the upper door opens against the sky, are sudden, brief, and gone, delivered from the close hands of the present.
the-story-of-the-gadsbys:
Rudyard Kipling frames these Indian tales of the Gadsbys with a preface addressed to Captain J. Mafflin of the Duke of Derry's Pink Hussars. Kipling says he wrote the story as an awful warning. Mafflin disregarded it. He followed Gadsby's example into marriage. He paid a lost bet at once. He also turned his wife against the author. Kipling is now barred from their door, darwaza band.

The mock grievance runs through dinner at the club. A mail-phaeton and housekeeping talk follow. Then Kipling hands the book back to its source. The man supplied most of its material in freer bachelor days. A contents list names the pieces, from Poor Dear Mamma and The World Without through The Tents of Kedar, Fatima, and The Valley of the Shadow to The Swelling of Jordan.
the-summer-holidays: Amerel wrote this story for children, published by D. Appleton and Company in New York in 1851. Only the title pages and the opening of a contents list appear in this record. The opening chapters have varied settings. One sits in Uncle Harvey's parlor. One takes an evening walk. One visits Daddy Hall. Uncle Harvey's talk about rain follows. Thomas kills a hawk. A chapter about bats closes the heads. The children's holiday story itself does not appear.
the-thrall-of-leif-the-lucky-a-story-of-: Ottilie A. Liljencrantz wrote The Thrall of Leif the Lucky, a story of Viking days, and this record gives its title and contents without the tale itself. Thirteen chapters run from a country where wolves thrive better than lambs, through a maid in a silver helmet, a gallant outlaw, and a Viking lair. Leif appears as cross-bearer, and Eric the Red waits in his domain near the end. The headings promise Norse adventure in Greenland and Vinland country, while Liljencrantz's chapters remain outside the pages present.
the-unseen-world-and-other-essays:
John Fiske dedicates his essay collection to James Sime in a letter dated from Harvard University on February 3, 1876. Midnight talks in London and a May holiday on the Thames, he says, led him to write about the unseen world. The dozen papers added behind the title essay are, in his phrase, a clearing out of his workshop.

Contents pages list fourteen pieces in all. Early essays treat death's tomorrow, the Jesus of history, the Christ of dogma, miracles, and Draper on science and religion. Later ones turn historical and literary: the Bengal famine of 1770, Spain and the Netherlands, Longfellow's Dante, Paine's St. Peter, a philosophy of art, and Athenian and American life compared.
the-uses-of-diversity-a-book-of-essays: G. K. Chesterton's The Uses of Diversity was first published by Methuen in London in 1920, subtitled a book of essays. A list of his earlier books faces the title page, including Charles Dickens, Tremendous Trifles, and The Ballad of the White Horse. The material present here stops at the front matter and the start of the contents, so the essays themselves do not appear. Only the first contents entry, On Seriousness, beginning at page one, can be read in this record. The collection's other subjects remain unlisted here.
the-valiant-runaways:
Gertrude Atherton dedicates her yarn to George and Gilbert Jones, whose encouragement got it finished. Her hero, Roldan Castanada, paces his father's verandah in a red silk sash and silver spurs. Around him stretches Rancho Los Palos Verdes, level as a calm sea, where his father ranks among the wealthiest grandees in the Californias and thousands of cattle graze.

News has thrown the boy into confusion: soldiers are out gathering conscripts and may reach the rancho by evening. Roldan dreads conscription, though nobody could call him a coward. He has thrown bulls, ridden alone at night after a strayed colt, and defended himself before. Atherton builds a rich Spanish-California setting before the running away begins.
the-widow-o-callaghan-s-boys: Gulielma Zollinger, author of The Widow O'Callaghan's Boys, also wrote The Route of the Packing Houses and is identified as Anna Gulielma Zollinger. The pages present here give the title page and contents, so the story itself does not appear. Ten chapters run from five boys and one woman through poorhouse alley and a house divided. An unanswered question, a letter from Cornelius, and Good Luck, bad luck follow. Later headings promise what a mocking bird did, one more black Sunday, and a boy's scheme that grandpa joins.
their-yesterdays:
Harold Bell Wright, author of The Winning of Barbara Worth, published Their Yesterdays with illustrations by F. Graham Cootes. A dedication dated June 8, 1912 praises Mrs. Elsbery W. Reynolds and her children. A passage from Pope's Essay on Man frames life as a round of toys.

The proem begins simply with a man who keeps returning to his past days. A woman does the same, again and again. Wright presents that shared habit as common to every reader. The opening sets up a reflective novel about memory, age, and the lives people revisit in thought.
three-plays:
Zora Neale Hurston's Three Plays gathers Lawing and Jawing, Forty Yards, and Woofing, transcribed from her original manuscripts. Pencilled notations, possibly Hurston's own, are marked as handwritten in the text. The first play is set at a way-cross in Georgia, in Judge Dunfumy's court.

Its people include Officer Simpson, Jemima Flapcakes, Cliff Mullins, John Barnes, two lawyers, a clerk, and a pretty girl with her escort. A large red arrow points offstage left, marked in the setting. Readers get Hurston's folk drama in manuscript form, with courtroom comedy rooted in Black southern speech and custom.
three-wonder-plays: Lady Gregory's Three Wonder Plays is introduced by long lists of her other works, from Seven Short Plays and folk-history plays to Cuchulain of Murthemne and Gods and Fighting Men. G. P. Putnam's Sons published the volume at London and New York. A note records copyright in the United States and Great Britain. Her Irish folklore and legend books fill one list, drama another. What is shown in this record stops with those lists and the copyright note, so Gregory's three wonder plays themselves do not appear.
tiger-and-tom-and-other-stories-for-boys: Tiger and Tom and Other Stories for Boys was compiled from Sabbath Readings, a four-volume set gathered from church papers of the 1870s. Publishers issued this illustrated reproduction in 1910 and call every story a lesson. Contents promise tales about scars, coals of fire, a faithful shepherd boy, disobedience, and standing by the ship. An illustration shows Tiger and Tom waiting faithfully in a marketplace each morning. The publishers' note and contents are what is shown in this record, so the stories themselves do not appear.
tom-brown-s-school-days:
Thomas Hughes prepared his school story from a 1905 Nelson edition, and part one opens with the Brown family. Hughes celebrates the Browns as an illustrious English clan, lately sung by Thackeray and Doyle. For centuries, he says, they subdued the earth in English counties and left marks in American forests and Australian uplands.

Brown sons fought at Cressy and Agincourt, against Spaniards and Dutchmen, and under Nelson and Wellington, taking hard knocks and little praise. Hughes, a devout Brown-worshipper connected to the family, wants to right their neglect. Readers get the famous Rugby school novel framed as a tribute to ordinary English stock.
trifles-for-the-christmas-holidays: H. S. Armstrong's Trifles for the Christmas Holidays came out at Philadelphia from J. B. Lippincott in 1869. Armstrong dedicates the pieces to Jas. Davidson Hill of New Orleans, a schoolfellow, comrade in arms, and friend of later years. The copyright was entered in 1868 in Louisiana. The contents begin with The Overture and A Christmas Melody. Only the title page, dedication, and start of the contents are present here, so the holiday pieces themselves do not appear.
tropic-days:
E. J. Banfield's Tropic Days, dated 1918, continues the island sketches of The Confessions of a Beachcomber and My Tropic Isle. His author's note addresses brother beachcombers. Earlier books, he says, gave exact details of life on an island off North Queensland, where some original inhabitants kept their old ways.

Banfield insists he describes Aboriginal people as men and women, not ethnological specimens, though a tint of imagination warms the truths. He thanks museum men at Sydney and Brisbane for help with his notes. Part one, Sun Days, lists pieces on idle moments, eternal sunshine, fragrance and fruit, and quiet waters. Dunk Island readers get slow, sunlit observation.
utopia-of-usurers-and-other-essays: Gilbert Keith Chesterton wrote the essays in Utopia of Usurers. The pages here give the contents list and the first lines of an opening poem, so the essays themselves do not appear. The contents promise pieces on art and advertising, and on letters and new poets. Other titles name the war on holidays, the church of the servile state, and science and the eugenists. The opening poem, A Song of Swords, retells a newspaper scrap about rioters who stopped a drove of cattle in an Irish village called Swords.
vanishing-roads-and-other-essays:
Richard Le Gallienne published Vanishing Roads and Other Essays in 1915. A long letter to his friend Robert Hobart Davis fronts the book. The letter calls the two of them fellow wayfarers on the vanishing road of the world, within hailing distance for many years. Le Gallienne says Davis shares more than an editor's share in some of the essays. His quick mind, and his early welcome, both helped.

The letter also tells a life in brief. As a boy in England, Le Gallienne dreamed of America as a promised land. He little guessed it would become his home in fact and in spirit, and the last resting place of his household gods. That warmth colors the essays that follow. They look back along roads that fade as they are travelled. Readers get a gentle essayist in a mood of thanks, memory, and mild regret.
washington-square-plays:
Washington Square Plays, volume twenty of the Drama League Series, gathers four one-act plays from the Washington Square Players, issued by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1925. The plays are The Clod by Lewis Beach, Eugenically Speaking by Edward Goodman, Overtones by Alice Gerstenberg, and Helena's Husband by Philip Moeller. Edward Goodman, the company's director, adds a preface, and Walter Prichard Eaton an introduction.

Eaton opens on the stiff habits of the theatre. The world need not fear radicals there, he says, since a radical fights the whole dead weight of society, and nowhere more than in the playhouse. A man who pays for his amusement wants to be amused, and what pleases him, nine times out of ten, is what pleased him before. Against that weight, this little company staged new American one-act plays, and this volume keeps four of them in print for readers.
what-is-man-and-other-essays:
Mark Twain, born Samuel Langhorne Clemens, gathered essays in What Is Man? and Other Essays. The lead piece is a talk between an Old Man and a Young Man. The Old Man claims that a human being is only a machine. The Young Man asks him to give his grounds in full.

The talk starts with the stuff a steam engine is made of, down in the rocks as ore. Other pieces in the set cover the death of Jean, how to make dates stick, and tobacco. One essay asks if Shakespeare is dead. Readers find Twain at his most grave and his most sly in one volume.
wilderness-ways:
William J. Long wrote Wilderness Ways, the second series of his animal sketches, printed by Ginn in Boston in 1900. Long gave the book to a camp companion he calls Little Sweet-Voice. His preface says the sketches rest on years of watching in woods and fields. They study animals as animals, he insists, not as humans in fur.

No trait from man is needed to make a beast worth watching, Long argues. He gives both sides of wild life, its gentleness and its savagery. An ideal creature built from one sweet moment would cheat the reader, he says. Camp tales of birds and beasts follow, seen at close range. Honest watching is his method and his plea.
wolfville-days: Alfred Henry Lewis wrote this sequel volume of Wolfville tales. Pages present here hold only a publisher's header giving the title and his name, with a January 2003 release note. No title page, chapter list, or story text appears in these pages. The header alone cannot show which tales the volume holds or how they differ from the first Wolfville gathering.
woman-s-life-in-colonial-days: Carl Holliday, a professor of English, wrote this study of women's lives in colonial America. It was first printed in 1922. Pages present here hold the title page and a detailed chapter outline, but no chapter text. The first chapter outline covers colonial women and religion, early hardship, and the harsh preaching of Michael Wigglesworth and Jonathan Edwards. Later chapters, judging by the outline plan, follow women through home life, work, and war.
women-and-the-alphabet-a-series-of-essay:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson gathered these essays on women's education and rights in 1881. His opening essay asks whether women ought to learn the alphabet. It first ran in the Atlantic Monthly in 1859. Higginson notes a report that reading it led Sophia Smith to found a women's college at Northampton. That claim shows the essay's reach.

Other essays cover the body, temperament, and common sense about women. Many first appeared in the Woman's Journal. The volume later spread to London and into German translation. Readers get calm, reasoned arguments for wider schooling and fairer treatment of women.
worldly-ways-byways: Eliot Gregory, writing as An Idler, published these social essays with Scribner's in 1899. Pages present here hold the title page, his dedication letter to E. L. Godkin, and the start of a contents list. Gregory thanks Godkin for suggesting the volume. Listed essays cover charm, travel contrasts, gilded misalliances, and the complacency of mediocrity. The essay texts themselves do not appear in these pages.
yesterdays: Ella Wheeler Wilcox published this book of poems in London in 1910. Pages present here hold a contents list of poem titles, but no poems themselves. Titles such as An Old Heart, Warp and Woof, Courage, and Love's Burial suggest themes of love, loss, and endurance. Other titles promise lighter pieces, like a rondeau and a man's reverie. The verse itself does not appear in these pages, so tone and quality stay undescribed here.
young-lion-of-the-woods-or-a-story-of-ea:
Thomas B. Smith published this story of early colonial days at Halifax in 1889. He dedicated his first work to his wife. His preface claims one merit for the tale. It records facts about duty, faith, and liberty under hard testing, he says. Loyal people suffered much in the colony's founding years. Smith quotes praise for anyone who sets a colony on foot.

A poem by Chas. G. D. Roberts on the title page hails a patriot Canadian people. That patriotic frame shapes the whole story. Readers get colonial hardship told as a lesson in loyalty. Fact and sentiment blend by the author's own admission.
your-boys:
Gipsy Smith wrote this wartime appeal after six months living among British soldiers at the front. A foreword by the Bishop of London introduces it. Smith tells of preaching within forty yards of German lines. He slept in a cellar where his boots froze to the floor. Sour French bread and hot sugared milk water comforted him most, he says.

He praises Y. M. C. A. marquees serving walking wounded near the trenches. Ten thousand cases got hot drinks in three days at three marquees. One waiting colonel, haggard and cold, simply said to carry on. Smith argues Christian work means doing, not preaching alone.
youth-and-sex-dangers-and-safeguards-for: Mary Scharlieb and F. Arthur Sibly wrote this 1919 guide on sex dangers and safeguards for the young. Pages present here hold a contents list, but no chapter text. Scharlieb's part treats girls, covering bodily changes at puberty, duties toward teenage girls, sickness care, and mental training. Sibly's part treats boys, arguing that impurity is widespread and that sex knowledge can suit perfect innocence. Teaching conditions and cures close his part, per the contents.
